LLBPE: Linked-List Based
GPU-Parallel BPE Tokenizer

Aditya Kovilur Affiliation: aditya373@icloud.com
Texas A&M University
College Station, TX, USA    Varun Chandra Shekar Affiliation: vcs@tamu.edu
Texas A&M University
College Station, TX, USA    Ariful Azad Affiliation: ariful@tamu.edu
Texas A&M University
College Station, TX, USA
Abstract

Every LLM inference begins with tokenization, which converts raw input bytes into the discrete token sequence the model consumes. For text, this step is often implemented using Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), an algorithm originally introduced for data compression. BPE has traditionally run on the CPU with extensive optimization, but recent work has moved it to the GPU for higher throughput. We show that these GPU implementations are bottlenecked not by computation but by data movement. We develop LLBPE that represents the token sequence as an array-based linked list so that each merge reduces to a constant-time pointer update. Furthermore, LLBPE fuses rank lookup, minimum selection, and merging into a single kernel to eliminate redundant hash map queries. LLBPE achieves up to 5.2× higher throughput than the best existing GPU implementation and 24.6× over optimized CPU implementations, at the cost of minor discrepancies in tokenized output.

Index Terms: 
Tokenization, Natural Language Processing, High Performance Computing, Parallel Processing

I Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) sit at the center of contemporary machine learning, and their end-to-end inference pipelines have received extensive optimization. Every such pipeline begins with the same step. Raw input is split into discrete units called tokens before the model can process it. Although tokenization is not the dominant runtime cost of an individual forward pass, it is executed on every request, and its overhead accumulates significantly in high-volume serving environments. Accelerating tokenization is therefore critical for maximizing overall pipeline throughput.

Given its central role in natural language processing, various tokenization schemes have been developed, including WordPiece [1], SentencePiece [2], and Unigram [3]. Among these, Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) [4, 5] has emerged as the standard for modern LLMs, powering the GPT family [6] and leading open-weight models such as Llama [7]. Consequently, accelerating BPE through GPU parallelism is of high practical importance.

BPE tokenization has traditionally relied on highly optimized CPU implementations, such as OpenAI’s tiktoken [8] and Hugging Face Tokenizers [9]. However, CPU-based approaches are fundamentally constrained by host core counts and memory transfers. Recent efforts have sought to offload BPE to the GPU. BlockBPE [10] parallelizes merge passes within CUDA thread blocks, while GPUTOK [11] maps exact BPE merge rules directly to GPU hardware. Nevertheless, both methods maintain a flat array as their underlying sequence representation, severely limiting their performance scalability.

The primary performance bottleneck in current GPU algorithms lies in excessive data movement. In a flat array, merging two adjacent tokens requires closing the resulting gap, either by shifting all downstream elements (as in BlockBPE) or by copying the sequence to an auxiliary buffer (as in GPUTOK). Consequently, each merge incurs an O⁡(N)O(N) memory overhead relative to sequence length (NN). On a GPU, these global memory writes are far more expensive than the hash map lookups and rank comparisons that constitute the actual work of BPE.

We address this with Linked-List BPE (LLBPE), a parallel BPE algorithm that represents the token sequence as an array-based linked list rather than a flat array. In this setting, a merge becomes a constant-time pointer update touching only the two tokens being merged, leaving every other position untouched. We further fuse rank lookup, minimum selection, and merging into a single kernel so that each hash map value is retrieved once and reused. On our set of parameters, LLBPE achieves a peak throughput of 370 MB/s, a 5.2×\times improvement over GPUTOK at 71.3 MB/s, while introducing only minor discrepancies along thread-block boundaries.

This trade-off suits a growing class of deployments. As LLM serving diversifies into low-latency and high-volume configurations alongside deep reasoning workloads, throughput-sensitive settings increasingly prioritize faster processing at every pipeline stage over exact output fidelity. The same applies under heavy request loads, where sustaining throughput matters more than maximizing model accuracy.

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

  • •

    Bottleneck Analysis: We identify global data movement in flat-array token representations as the primary efficiency bottleneck in existing GPU BPE implementations.

  • •

    LLBPE Algorithm: We propose an array-based linked-list representation that reduces per-merge data movement from O⁡(N)O(N) to O⁡(1)O(1), and fuse candidate selection and merging into a single unified GPU kernel.

  • •

    Empirical Evaluation: We evaluate LLBPE against CPU baselines (tiktoken, Hugging Face Tokenizers) and GPU implementations (BlockBPE, GPUTOK). LLBPE achieves peak speedups of 5.2×5.2\times over prior GPU methods and 24.6×24.6\times over CPU-based implementations.

  • •

    Implementation: LLBPE is publicly available here. The setup is mentioned in the Artifact Description section in the appendix.

II Background

II-A Byte Pair Encoding

Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) was introduced by Gage [4] as a data compression algorithm. Given an input byte sequence, BPE repeatedly finds the most frequent adjacent pair of bytes, replaces every occurrence of that pair with a single unused byte, and records the substitution in a lookup table. This process repeats until no pair occurs more than once. The original sequence can be recovered by replaying the substitutions in reverse order.

As an example, consider the input string aaabdaaabac. The pair aa is the most frequent, so it is replaced by an unused symbol Z, yielding ZabdZabac with the table entry Z→aa\texttt{Z}{\rightarrow}\texttt{aa}. Next, the pair ab is most frequent. Replacing ab with Y produces ZYdZYac with the additional entry Y→ab\texttt{Y}\rightarrow\texttt{ab}. The process continues until no pair appears more than once.

Sennrich et al. [5] adapted BPE for subword tokenization in neural machine translation. It has since become the dominant tokenization method in large language models including GPT-4 [12] and LLaMA [13].

II-B Training and Encoding Phases

The use of BPE in LLMs typically involves two phases. In an offline training phase, a fixed-size vocabulary of merge rules is learned from a training corpus. Starting from a character-level (or byte-level) vocabulary, the algorithm repeatedly counts all adjacent token pairs across the corpus, merges the most frequent pair into a new token, and appends the rule to an ordered merge table. This repeats for a predetermined number of merges (e.g., 50,257 tokens for GPT-2 or 100,256 for GPT-4’s cl100k_base vocabulary). The goal of this training phase is to learn an ordered merge table that can be used to tokenize arbitrary text at inference time.

In the encoding (inference) phase, the tokenizer does not re-count frequencies of new input strings. Instead, it splits the input into bytes and iteratively scans for adjacent pairs that appear in the learned merge table. At each step, the pair with the lowest index (highest priority) in the ordered merge table is merged, regardless of how many times it occurs in the current input. This process repeats until no adjacent pair in the current sequence matches any entry in the merge table. Because every single byte is always a valid token in the vocabulary, BPE guarantees that any input can be encoded. This paper focuses exclusively on parallelizing the BPE encoding phase on the GPU, taking a pre-trained merge table as a fixed input.

II-C Pre tokenization

Modern tokenizers such as OpenAI’s tiktoken and HuggingFace Tokenizers also apply a regex-based pre-tokenization step before BPE merging. This step splits the input at word boundaries, whitespace, and punctuation using patterns such as GPT-2’s splitting regex, ensuring that merges do not cross word boundaries. Pre-tokenization typically accounts for a substantial fraction of total tokenization time and is one of the key challenges in moving BPE to the GPU, since regex evaluation involves backtracking and branching logic that resists parallelization.

III Related Work

III-A Tokenization Methods

Subword tokenization is a prerequisite for all modern LLMs, and three methods dominate in practice. BPE is the most widely used tokenization method in modern LLMs. It is used throughout the GPT family [6]. Recent open-weight models such as Llama 3 [7] also replaced the SentencePiece-BPE scheme of Llama 1/2 with a larger, tiktoken-style byte-level BPE vocabulary.

WordPiece is used by BERT-family models [14]. Unlike BPE, WordPiece performs a left-to-right greedy longest-match search against a learned vocabulary, consuming the longest recognized token at each position before advancing. It does not use a global merge priority and does not consider pairs at arbitrary positions in the string.

SentencePiece is a tokenization framework that supports both BPE and Unigram Language Model [15] backends. They use a single Viterbi (dynamic programming) pass to find the segmentation that maximizes the probability of the token distribution. The entire algorithm runs as one dynamic programming pass over the corpus, without a merging step at each iteration. Models such as T5 [3] and ALBERT [16] use SentencePiece with the Unigram backend.

III-B CPU-Based Implementations

Several optimized CPU implementations of BPE encoding exist in the literature. HuggingFace Tokenizers offers a Rust-based library supporting BPE, WordPiece, and Unigram backends with Python bindings. OpenAI’s tiktoken optimizes BPE encoding in Rust. fastBPE [17] provides a multithreaded C++ implementation with memory-mapped I/O.

III-C GPU-Accelerated Tokenization

Several recent efforts have targeted GPU acceleration of tokenization. The RAPIDS cuDF library [18] provides a GPU-based subword tokenizer for WordPiece in BERT pipelines. BlockBPE [10] proposes a parallel BPE implementation that replaces regex-based pre-tokenization with byte-level splitting to enable intra-block parallelism on the GPU GPUTOK [11] builds on similar ideas to implement GPT-2’s exact merge rules on the GPU.

IV Method

IV-A Pre Tokenization

Before applying BPE merges, the input text is split into pre-tokens such as words and numbers. Pre-tokenization enforces the semantic rules of the input language, thereby preserving contextual information. For example, a number such as 1000 should always be tokenized as a single unit rather than split into 10 and 00. Analogous rules govern punctuation, contractions, and similar constructs. Without this step, the string sample word could produce tokens such as samp, lewo, rd, merging the unrelated characters le and wo across a word boundary and introducing spurious context. Modern tokenizers implement pre-tokenization by lexing the input stream with a set of regular expressions that greedily form the longest valid pre-tokens.

BlockBPE removes pre-tokenization entirely to maximize GPU performance, at the cost of small deviations in tokenization output. Our implementation retains pre-tokenization but overlaps it with file I/O by processing the input as a stream, so that pre-tokenized spans are ready for GPU processing as soon as they are read from disk.

We implement pre-tokenization as a single linear scan over the input using a pre-computed trie that encodes the tokenizer’s regular expressions using the Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) algorithm [19]. In this approach, at each node, a valid input advances to a child node, while a mismatch follows a pre-computed failure link that falls back to the longest previously matched suffix. This ensures that every byte is visited at most a constant number of times. The time complexity of the scan is O⁡(N+P)O(N+P), where NN is the length of the input and PP is the maximum depth of the trie. In practice N≫PN\gg P, so the cost reduces to O⁡(N)O(N), which is the same asymptotic cost as simply copying the input into an array. The pre-tokenization overhead is therefore amortized over the cost of populating the token buffer that is subsequently transferred to the GPU.

IV-B Batching and Thread Mapping

We implement BPE on the GPU by partitioning the input text into batches. Each batch contains BATCH_SIZE (number of) substrings, and each substring is of length N=SEQ_LENN=\texttt{SEQ\_LEN} initial tokens (each token is a byte after pre-tokenization and before the first iteration of BPE). Hence, BATCH_SIZE×SEQ_LEN\texttt{BATCH\_SIZE}\times\texttt{SEQ\_LEN} is equal to the total number of bytes processed in one GPU kernel launch.

We assign each batch to its own thread block of NN threads. As a result, each thread is responsible for exactly one token at any given point during execution. Since block scheduling is handled by the CUDA scheduler, our algorithm centers around how each batch is processed within a thread block.

Since each thread handles exactly one token and we employ no thread coarsening (in contrast to BlockBPE), sequence length and batch size are not independent:

SEQ_LEN×BATCH_SIZE=MAX_THREADS,\texttt{SEQ\_LEN}\times\texttt{BATCH\_SIZE}=\texttt{MAX\_THREADS}, (1)

where MAX_THREADS is the hardware limit on the number of threads that the GPU can spawn concurrently. Due to the limitation of tokenizing an input of MAX_THREADS bytes at a time, for an input larger than that, we launch the GPU kernel multiple times. For example, if MAX_THREADS = 200,000 and the input text is of SIZE = 2,100,000 Bytes, we launch the GPU kernel ceil(SIZE / MAX_THREADS) = 11 times.

IV-C Overview of the Algorithm

The core of BPE encoding is a loop that repeatedly identifies the highest-priority adjacent token pair and merges it into a single token. In a flat array representation, each merge requires shifting all subsequent elements to close the gap. Such data shifting is expensive on the GPU, where global memory writes are costly. We instead emulate a linked list on the GPU, where each token stores indices to its successor.

Hence, a merge reduces to updating a constant number of index entries in this linked list. Each merge iteration consists of three steps, illustrated in Figure 1.

Step 1: Rank evaluation. For each adjacent pair in the current sequence, look up its merge rank in the pre-trained table. This step takes O⁡(N)O(N) time, where NN is the number of active tokens.

Step 2: Minimum selection. Find the pair with the lowest rank (highest priority). This can be performed via linear scan or tree-based reduction, both effectively O⁡(N)O(N) in the number of active tokens.

Step 3: Merge. Replace the selected pair with a single merged token and update the sequence.

The key difference between our approach and prior GPU implementations lies in Step 3. BlockBPE stores tokens in a flat array and shifts all elements after the merge position left by one, making Step 3 O⁡(N)O(N). GPUTOK uses a double-buffered array, copying all NN elements into a second buffer in every iteration, which is also O⁡(N)O(N). In LLBPE’s linked-list representation, Step 3 is O⁡(1)O(1) because exactly one thread updates the merged token’s value and redirects its successor pointer to skip the consumed neighbor.

IV-D Data Structures

LLBPE relies on two GPU-resident data structures: a hash map encoding the pre-trained merge table and a pair of parallel arrays representing the token sequence as a linked list.

Merge Tables. We store the merge table as a GPU-resident hash map using cuCollections, passed as a parameter to the merge kernel. Each entry of the hash map encodes a token pair and its merge rule in two 64-bit integers:

  1. 1.

    Key (64-bit unsigned integer): The upper 32 bits store tokeni\text{token}_{i} and the lower 32 bits store tokeni+1\text{token}_{i+1}, packing an adjacent pair into a single 64-bit lookup key.

  2. 2.

    Value (64-bit unsigned integer): The upper 32 bits store the merge rank and the lower 32 bits store the resulting merged token ID.

This value layout, also used by GPUTOK, has a useful property. Because the rank occupies the upper bits, a numeric minimum over raw 64-bit values is equivalent to selecting the lowest rank. The minimum simultaneously yields both the winning rank and the corresponding merged token ID in a single comparison, with no additional lookup required. Since all ranks in the merge table are distinct, ties cannot occur.

Token Sequence. The token sequence is represented as a linked list using two parallel arrays:

  • •

    tokens[i]: the ID of the ii-th token in the current sequence.

  • •

    nextToken[i]: the index of the successor of position ii in the tokens array. A value of −1-1 indicates a deleted node (consumed by a merge) or the end of a pre-token boundary.

Each thread owns exactly one position in the linked list, accessing only its corresponding entries in the tokens and next arrays. This one-to-one mapping eliminates memory access conflicts between threads and ensures coalesced reads when thread indices are contiguous. A merge operation updates at most three entries, leaving all other array positions untouched.

IV-E The Merge Iteration

Each merge iteration identifies the adjacent token pair with the lowest merge rank, merges it into a single token, and updates the linked list accordingly. Algorithm 1 shows the complete iteration, executed by every thread in parallel. Rank lookup, minimum selection, and the merge itself are fused into a single kernel so that the hash map value retrieved in Phase 1 can be reused in Phase 3 without a second query.

Phase 1: Rank lookup (lines 1–6). A thread is active in a given iteration if nextToken​[i]≠−1\texttt{nextToken}[i]\neq-1, meaning a prior merge has not consumed its token and it has a valid successor to form a pair with. Each active thread looks up its adjacent pair (tokens​[i],tokens​[j])(\texttt{tokens}[i],\;\texttt{tokens}[j]) in the hash map, where j=nextToken​[i]j=\texttt{nextToken}[i], and caches the returned 64-bit value. The thread then constructs a candidate word by masking off the lower 32 bits of the value and substituting its own position ii, leaving the rank in place in the upper 32 bits.

In principle, only two pairs change between iterations (the pair formed by the newly merged token and its successor, and the pair formed by the predecessor and the newly merged token), so unchanged pairs could skip this lookup. As an optimization, all active threads perform the lookup during initialization. On subsequent iterations, only the threads whose pairs were modified by the previous merge repeat it, while the rest reuse their cached values. This reduces the number of hash map queries per iteration from O⁡(N)O(N) to O⁡(1)O(1) after initialization.

Phase 2: Atomic minimum selection (lines 7–14). Every active thread attempts to insert its candidate into the shared-memory variable minRP using an atomic compare-and-swap (CAS) loop. Because the rank occupies the upper 32 bits, a numeric comparison on the packed word is equivalent to comparing by rank and breaking ties by position. Since all merge ranks are distinct, the final value of minRP uniquely identifies both the winning rank and the merge position.

Note that our reduction is asymptotically similar to the tree-based reduction used in GPUTOK which has O⁡(N)O(N) time complexity. However, we found that the tree-based approach introduces multiple synchronization barriers per iteration, which makes it expensive in practice. By contrast, our flat atomic approach avoids inter-thread synchronization entirely, relying instead on atomic operations that are efficiently serialized by the hardware.

Phase 3: Merge (lines 15–21). After a barrier synchronization, every thread reads the winning position from the lower 32 bits of minRP. The thread whose position matches performs the merge. In the merging phase, the thread extracts the merged token ID from the lower 32 bits of its cached hash map value, writes it to tokens​[i]\texttt{tokens}[i], redirects nextToken​[i]\texttt{nextToken}[i] past the consumed neighbor jj, and sets nextToken​[j]←−1\texttt{nextToken}[j]\leftarrow-1 to mark jj as deleted. Both jj and the cached value are per-thread registers held since Phase 1, so no additional memory reads or hash map queries are needed.

Figure 2 illustrates the merging process with an example. If the pair "h", "i" has the highest merge priority, the two tokens merge to form "hi" and thread #2 becomes inactive for all subsequent iterations. Only the pairs {"w", "hi"} and {"hi", "c"} require new rank lookups in the following iteration (Figure 2(b)).

Block-boundary handling. We restrict merging within each thread block because cross-block merges require expensive inter-block synchronization through global memory barriers, which significantly reduces tokenization throughput. Consequently, pairs that straddle a block boundary are never merged, which can yield tokenizations that differ from a strictly serial implementation. Section V-B quantifies how often this occurs and its effect on tokenization quality.

V Experiments

V-A Experimental Settings

Dataset

We evaluate the tokenizer on several corpora drawn from Tolstoy’s War and Peace[20], Mark Twain’s Tom Sawyer [21], and Huckleberry Finn [22]. The sizes of all these datasets are discussed in Table I.

Platform

All experiments were run on a GPU node of the Perlmutter supercomputer at NERSC. Specifically, we used an NVIDIA A100 GPU with 80GB of memory, paired with an AMD EPYC 7763 CPU (64 cores, 256GB DDR4 DRAM). Perlmutter uses a PCIe 4.0 interconnect for the CPU-GPU data transfer with a bidirectional bandwidth of 64GBps. The A100 supports approximately 200K concurrently resident threads, which upper-bounds the product of sequence length and batch size in our experiments.

Configuration

We use CUDA 12.9 and gcc-native 12.3 for compilation. We also use cmake 3.30.4 for compiling cuCollections with the corresponding version of CUDA. We use the GPT-2 [23] tokenization vocabulary and merge table for all baselines and LLBPE.

Baselines

We compare against tiktoken and HuggingFace. These are CPU-based implementations; hence, we run them on the AMD EPYC 7763 CPU as mentioned above. BlockBPE and GPUTOK are GPU implementations and are tested on NVIDIA A100. As there is no publicly available implementation of the original BlockBPE paper, we use the BlockBPE implementation from GPUTOK. Tiktoken, HuggingFace, and BlockBPE are Rust implementations with Python interfaces. GPUTOK and LLBPE are C++ implementations.

V-B Tokenization Quality

Since our aim is not to improve tokenization accuracy, we instead evaluate how closely our tokenizer’s output matches that of the trusted HuggingFace BPE tokenizer, which we adopt as the reference. The goal is to show that LLBPE tokenization matches closely with the HuggingFace BPE tokenizer.

Following the methodology of BlockBPE, we quantify the similarity between two tokenizers’ outputs by computing the normalized Levenshtein distance between our output and that of HuggingFace. For each input string sis_{i}, the similarity score is defined as:

sim​(si)=1−dL​(tiHF,tiLL)|si|,\text{sim}(s_{i})=1-\frac{d_{L}\!\left(t_{i}^{\text{HF}},\,t_{i}^{\text{LL}}\right)}{|s_{i}|}, (2)

where dL​(tiHF,tiLL)d_{L}(t_{i}^{\text{HF}},t_{i}^{\text{LL}}) is the Levenshtein distance [24] between the HuggingFace tokenization tiHFt_{i}^{\text{HF}} and the LLBPE tokenization tiLLt_{i}^{\text{LL}} for string sis_{i}, and |si||s_{i}| denotes the number of tokens in sis_{i}. Here, the Levenshtein distance measures the minimum number of single-token insertions, deletions, and substitutions required to transform one token sequence into the other, providing a standard measure of edit-based dissimilarity between two sequences. A similarity score of 1 indicates that the two tokenizations are identical, while lower values indicate a greater number of edits needed to reconcile the two outputs. The final similarity is reported as the mean of sim​(si)\text{sim}(s_{i}) over all chunks in the corpus.

Figure 3 shows that LLBPE is comparable to HuggingFace BPE, with similarity scores close to 99% for Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, and 96% for War and Peace. We note that these differences do not indicate inferior accuracy on the part of LLBPE. They simply mean that LLBPE generates slightly different tokens than HuggingFace does.

The reason for these differences is that token pairs lying at block boundaries are not compared across blocks when evaluating merge rank in order to ensure that the algorithm operates strictly within a block for high performance. Consequently, certain merges are missed whenever a boundary token pair has the highest merge priority, introducing a discrepancy between the algorithm’s output and the ground-truth tokenization. This does not cause any data loss, as it merely leaves some tokens split at the block boundary.

Figure 3 also reveals that similarity improves with a higher sequence length. This is expected because a higher sequence length results in a smaller batch size for a fixed thread budget. This corresponds to fewer blocks on the GPU and consequently fewer block boundaries, reducing the opportunities for merges to be missed at those boundaries.

V-C Tokenization Throughput

We define throughput as the number of bytes a tokenizer processes per unit time, reported in MB/s. Formally, given a corpus of total size BB bytes and a measured runtime tt (in seconds), throughput is computed as

Throughput (MB/s)=B106×t,\text{Throughput (MB/s)}=\frac{B}{10^{6}\times t}, (3)

where BB denotes the total number of bytes in the corpus and tt denotes the runtime of the program.

We compare LLBPE with two widely used CPU baselines, tiktoken and Hugging Face, and two recently developed GPU BPE implementations, BlockBPE and GPUTOK. As discussed previously, the product of batch size and sequence length equals the maximum number of threads in LLBPE. Consequently, as sequence length increases, batch size decreases proportionally. Figure 4 presents the throughput results across various sequence lengths.

All reported numbers in Figure 4 correspond to the merge kernel, which does not include the file I/O required for reading the corpus. The GPU-based baselines skip pre-tokenization, hence the results shown are a direct comparison between the merge kernels. However, the CPU-based baselines run pre-tokenization as the first step on a string buffer passed as input after the corpus is read. Since we perform pre-tokenization on a streamed input, we were unable to show a direct comparison of the effect of pre-tokenization on the end to end execution time with the CPU-based baselines.

Overall throughput

Figure 4 shows that the GPU tokenizers, LLBPE, BlockBPE, and GPUTOK, consistently perform much better than the highly-optimized CPU tokenizers from OpenAI and HuggingFace, across all batch sizes and sequence lengths. This is not surprising, given the massive parallelization available on the GPU compared to multicore CPUs. Between the CPU baselines, tiktoken achieves higher throughput than HuggingFace across all experiments. Between the two GPU baselines, GPUTOK slightly outperforms BlockBPE. However, across all experiments, LLBPE performs significantly better than both GPUTOK and BlockBPE. In the best case (sequence length 128), LLBPE achieves a throughput of 370 MB/s, which is 7×7\times faster than GPUTOK and ∼20×\sim 20\times faster than tiktoken. In the worst case (sequence length 1024), LLBPE achieves 38.7 MB/s, which is 2×2\times faster than GPUTOK and ∼2.5×\sim 2.5\times faster than tiktoken. Hence, LLBPE performs the best overall across all configurations explored in this paper.

Throughput with respect to Sequence length

Sweeping across various sequence lengths, we notice much higher throughput values for lower sequence lengths and higher batch sizes. The difference between the throughputs at sequence lengths 128 and 1024 is an order of magnitude, and this can be attributed to the warp scheduling having a lower overhead for shorter sequence lengths. The most expensive step of LLBPE is the global memory access for merge ranks, which triggers a warp scheduler to hide the latency caused by it. A shorter sequence length corresponds to a smaller block size, i.e. a sequence length of 128 would correspond to 128 threads in each GPU block. Consequently, it has a direct impact on the number of warps within a block. Therefore, the shorter the sequence length, the fewer the warps within a GPU, which leads to easier latency-hiding scheduling between warps. This is because block scheduling takes precedence once all warps are idle, which happens sooner if there are fewer warps.

VI Conclusion

We presented LLBPE, a GPU-accelerated BPE tokenizer that achieves a peak throughput of 370 MB/s (with our configuration), a 5.2×\times improvement over the next best baseline, GPUTOK, at 71.3 MB/s. The performance gain follows from a single design principle. Because BPE encoding involves only hash map lookups and rank comparisons, its cost on the GPU is dominated by data movement rather than computation. LLBPE minimizes this movement by representing the token sequence as an array-based linked list, reducing each merge from an O⁡(N)O(N) array shift to an O⁡(1)O(1) pointer update. Additionally, LLBPE fuses rank lookup, minimum selection, and merging into a single kernel so that hash map values retrieved once are reused without re-querying global memory.

Although tokenization is not the dominant cost of LLM inference, it is performed on every input and at high frequency in serving pipelines. Accelerating it on the GPU also keeps token sequences resident in device memory, avoiding host-to-device transfers in workloads where the downstream model already runs on the GPU.

LLBPE has one notable limitation. Merges are confined to thread block boundaries, so pairs straddling adjacent blocks are never merged. This introduces minor discrepancies relative to the reference HuggingFace tokenizer output, and in this work, we do not study the impact of this difference in the downstream tasks of LLMs. Extending LLBPE to resolve cross-block merges without sacrificing throughput, for example through a lightweight boundary fix-up pass, is a natural direction for future work.

Abstract

This artifact contains the implementation for LLBPE in C++. We provide instructions on generating results for Figures 3, 4.

Artifact Description

: The code for LLBPE can be found here. The testing was done on an NVIDIA A100 GPU on NERSC’s Perlmutter on an interactive GPU node. The setup instructions for our platform are mentioned below and can also be found in README.md in the root directory.

Note: The project can be compiled using the script in scripts/build.sh. The executable generated by running the build script is present in build/ and can be run with the following arguments: .

⬇
./build/LLBPE <input-file> \
<output-file|stdout> <mode(SEQ|BATCH)> \
<mode-value>
  1. 1.

    input-file: File address of the corpus to tokenize

  2. 2.

    output-file: File address to store the tokenized output

  3. 3.

    mode: SEQ/BATCH to specify which parameter is fixed

    1. (a)

      SEQ: sequence length

    2. (b)

      BATCH: batch size

  4. 4.

    mode-value: Value of the parameter specified in ¡mode¿

Modules

These commands and versions are specific to the platform on which we run our tests.

⬇
module load cuda # CUDA 12.9
module load gcc-native/12.3
module unload cray-mpich
module load mpich

Build

The commands provided below are included in the build script:

⬇
mkdir -p build
cd ./build
cmake ..
make
